subject: economics
title: Externalities
welcome_lead: Markets miss the costs and benefits felt by third parties.
meta_desc: A-Level Market Failure: positive and negative externalities.
final_note: Markets ignore third-party effects - that is the textbook market failure.

concepts.def: Free market produces an allocation that is not Pareto efficient; sources include externalities, public goods, information failure.
Where price diverges from marginal social cost; creates deadweight loss.
Akerlof (1970) Market for Lemons: used car buyers know less than sellers, causing market unravelling.
Insured parties take more risk because they don't bear full costs; explains 2008 banking crisis behaviour.
Low-quality buyers/sellers crowd out high-quality due to information asymmetry; insurance markets vulnerable.
Goods with positive externalities under-consumed by free market; e.g. vaccines, education.

walkthroughs.body_html: A pollutant harms neighbours who never bought the good - that is a negative externality. A vaccine protects others - a positive externality. Either way the market price ignores them.
With a negative externality, MSC exceeds MPC and the market overproduces. With a positive externality, MSB exceeds MPB and the market underproduces.
Taxes (Pigouvian) shift MPC up to MSC. Subsidies shift MPB up to MSB. Tradable permits cap quantity. Property rights (Coase) let parties bargain.

A negative externality is something bad that happens to a business.
Demand always falls when supply increases.
A cost imposed on a third party not involved in the transaction — e.g. pollution from a factory affects neighbours who didn't choose to bear it.
A negative externality is a tax on a business.

mcqs.q: What is asymmetric information as a source of market failure?
options: Asymmetric information is when a market only operates in one direction.
Demand always falls when supply increases.
Asymmetric information means a buyer and seller disagree about a price.

When one party in a transaction knows more than the other — leading to problems like adverse selection (used-car market) or moral hazard (insurance). Markets can fail or unravel when information is unequal.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: Demand always falls when supply increases.
A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
A negative externality is a tax on a business.
A change in price shifts the demand curve.
